#7881. 18 Easy Bean Recipes For Dinner That Are Cheap & Nutritious

For a couple bucks a bag? You can’t beat ‘em.

Like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...). Since when did a pound of 80/20 become a special little treat? We’ve been opting for ground chicken and ground turkey instead for a few years now. As grocery prices continue to go up, what are you turning to to keep your own food bills down? Maybe it’s rice or lentils, but don’t forget about the humble bean. Canned beans and especially dried bagged beans are affordable sources of protein and fiber, and with the right bean recipes for dinner, you can make them so incredibly delicious. Here’s how to load them up with flavor.

Stuffed peppers are such a flavorful dish that even if you’re a meat-eater, you’ll never miss it in this recipe from All The Healthy Things. Don’t be intimidated by the long ingredient list — most of them are just seasonings you most likely have in your pantry already. These only take about 15 minutes of prep, then just pop them in the oven and go help with homework or baths ‘til they’re done.

Burrito bowls are easy, and they never disappoint. Princess Pinky Girls’ recipe clearly includes chicken, but honestly, if you sub in some really tasty refried beans or something, you won’t even miss it. We are big on burrito bowls in my house because they’re also great work lunches to prep ahead of time.

Chickpeas, aka garbanzo beans, are the filling base to this super flavorful Italian chickpea salad from Foodie Crush. With all the additions — red onion, bell pepper, garlic, pepperoncini, and more — this is a delicious dense bean salad that’ll just get better as the flavors meld together in the fridge all week long.

Averie Cooks’ Mediterranean white bean salad looks exactly like what I mean when I say I want a little snack, but can’t find anything I actually want in the fridge (it’s because I’m looking for a restaurant-quality appetizer at all times). This recipe is a bit more involved, but the marinated white beans, crispy asparagus, and shallots served over whipped ricotta sound good enough to be worth the trouble.

If you’re trying to up your fiber intake, Damn Delicious’ spinach and white bean soup is the recipe for you. This delicious dish is ready in 30 minutes and would be so, so good with some Parmesan grated on top and a side of crusty bread.

Chili is a major crowd-pleaser, and it’s a cheap way to make a lot of food at once, especially if you’re subbing in beans for beef. All The Healthy Things’ recipe includes meat, but you can just leave it out. That said, don’t skip the little dash of cocoa powder — it’s a game-changer.

Being able to make some simple but delicious bean sides yourself is a great way to save money, and fortunately, Simply LaKita’s Southern baked beans fit the bill. It takes about an hour, but you’ll have a big batch to pair with other proteins throughout the week.

I’m not sure falafel can be improved upon, but it’s fun to find out. What Jew Wanna Eat’s black bean falafel can be ready in about 20 minutes and doesn’t require many ingredients to pull off. Topped with tomatoes, cucumbers, and tzatziki, this is an easy and filling meal you’ll return to again and again.

If you’re having a bummer of a week, a cheesy, saucy enchilada night is guaranteed to make you feel at least 1% better. This version from Averie Cooks is a fantastic way to get more veggies into you and your kids, because the sweet potatoes and corn inside will indeed be coated in cheesy deliciousness.

Need a light, yummy salad to eat with chips for lunch? Or something easy to throw into burrito bowls or wraps? All The Healthy Things’ black bean and corn salad is easy to customize with your favorite veggies and herbs, and you can eat it in so many ways.

Filling, cheap taco ideas, you say? Damn Delicious has you covered with these black bean and quinoa tacos. They’re simple, satisfying, and inexpensive — the kind of recipe I could see going platinum in my house, personally.

Foodie Crush’s cannellini beans are another flavorful side you can pair with salads, proteins, or put on toast if you’re into that sort of thing. Or if you’re a fan of brothy beans, you can just grab the pot and a big spoon and dive in.

Princess Pinky Girl is the best at quick, easy recipes that are a breeze to make and super satisfying to eat. This cowboy casserole is also a one-pan meal (love) — it’s sort of like a chili base topped with cornbread. While her recipe calls for ground beef, you could easily just sub in extra beans and veggies.

Haute & Healthy Living’s Italian soup is rich and creamy thanks to a little coconut milk, and incredibly rich in flavor (shout-out to sun-dried tomatoes). The whole thing takes about 15 minutes of prep, and then the slow cooker will handle the rest for you.

These black bean burgers from Barefoot in the Pines take 35 minutes start to finish (hello, weeknight dinner MVP) and only take two cans of black beans, an onion, and some seasonings to pull off. You can top them with classic burger fixings or go with salsa and guac, as pictured here.

Fried plantains make a regular bowl of beans and rice feel special all of a sudden. This bowl by Cadry’s Kitchen is an easy, affordable meal that gets you all your food groups in one sitting. Like, if you had a nutritionist, they’d be so proud of you.

I love a side of restaurant-style refried beans, but I never think to make them at home. Haute & Healthy Living’s version will help you keep the sodium in check without sacrificing flavor. Eat these as a side, a dip, or load up some bean and cheese burritos.

Beans and rice is a complete meal, and a delicious one at that. This recipe from Biscuits & Burlap is a copycat of Popeye’s red beans and rice side, which, if you’re from the South, you know they’ve got some of the best around.

Which bean dishes will you fall back on to save a few bucks each week?

#7880. 48 Bulldogs, One Apartment, and a Disturbing Secret

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

This is exactly why we are against puppy mills.

Forty-eight dogs â mostly French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs â found in what authorities are describing as a clandestine breeding operation in San Juan de Miraflores, Peru.

And when you read what was found, it is hard not to feel angry.

Authorities discovered the animals in appalling conditions on September 28 in an apartment on JirÃ³n Santiago RodrÃ­guez. The group included 25 French Bulldogs, nine English Bulldogs, eight mixed-breed dogs, five French Bulldog puppies, and one Dachshund. There was also a rooster. Local French Bulldog club, Club Frenchie, heard about the rescue through social media and immediately reached out to offer assistance. One member of the club spoke to a reporter from the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio about what they had witnessed:

âThe state of health was absolutely deplorable. There were dogs covered in feces, filthy, with no hygiene whatsoever, dogs with broken nails, bitten ears, and other serious problems,â he said.

The dogs were brought to the Municipal Veterinary Clinic in San Juan de Miraflores, where they were examined and received treatment for a range of conditions. Most were suffering from heat stress, and many had excessively long nails, some bleeding, skin problems, fungal issues, eye infections, surgical scars, and other conditions requiring medical attention. Six puppies reportedly needed incubator care, with two described as being in a particularly fragile condition.

Following the intervention, the animals were taken to the municipal veterinary service, and some have since been moved into foster care. The San Juan de Miraflores Provincial Corporate Criminal Prosecutor's Office is investigating the case, and FÃ©lix Sonco and Darlys Vanegas were arrested at the scene.

As if the horrendous conditions that greeted rescuers werenât disturbing enough, it appears that this wasnât simply a breeding operation, but an illegal, makeshift veterinary clinic.

Some of these dogs had undergone surgery on their vocal cords; a barbaric procedure known as debarking. Being kept in cramped and filthy conditions meant that these dogs were barking and crying constantly. Debarking was a way to reduce noise and avoid complaints.

They didnât improve conditions. They didnât provide relief. They simply removed their ability to voice their distress.

Evidence also suggests that several female Bulldogs were bred repeatedly, with some reportedly forced to carry as many as ten litters of puppies. Veterinary examination also found evidence that crude cesarean surgeries had been performed prematurely to get puppies out faster and back on the market, while the mothers, if they survived, were bred again.

Investigators reportedly found premature newborn puppies inside an unsterilized incubator, while puppies were being sold for around 1,500 to 2,500 Peruvian soles each â roughly $400 to $670 USD.

French Bulldogs and English Bulldogs are brachycephalic breeds. Their shortened skull and squishy faces are a big part of their appeal. But there is a very uncomfortable truth behind that cute face.

That same anatomy that many people find irresistible can make it harder for a dog to breathe, exercise, sleep, regulate their body temperature, and, in some cases, give birth.

We have to stop pretending these things are simply âpart of being a Bulldog.â

A dog struggling to breathe is not just a snorer. A dog that overheats easily is not just âsensitive to the heat.â These are medical problems.

Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome (BOAS) refers to the conditions that affect breeds with a shortened skull, or âbrachycephaly.â These conditions include hypoplastic trachea (narrow  windpipe), stenotic nares (narrow nostrils), and a tongue and soft palate that are too large and long for the mouth, resulting in obstruction of the airways and difficulty swallowing.

These issues have led many veterinary professionals and animal welfare advocates to question the ethics of breeding these dogs. When a physical characteristic can affect basic functions like breathing and temperature regulation, choosing which dogs reproduce needs to consider more than appearance.

That little flat face. Those big eyes. The stout little body. The funny little snorts.

Most people see cute, even adorable. But as veterinarians, we see a whole list of problems that need to be monitored.

A Bulldog can be an absolutely wonderful companion and still have anatomy that puts them at risk for serious health problems. Breeding of these dogs should require more responsibility, not less, with breeders selecting for less extreme conformations.

There is something very sad about how much importance we place on how dogs look. A certain face. A certain size. A certain coat. A certain breed.

The more desirable that look becomes, the more money there is in producing it. That creates a market, and unfortunately, where there is money, there will always be those willing to cut corners.

This does not mean that every breeder is bad. There are responsible breeders who health-test their dogs, carefully select breeding pairs, provide appropriate veterinary care, and take responsibility for the puppies they bring into the world. Those who are actively trying to breed healthier versions of dogs whose health and function have been crippled through selective breeding for exaggerated features.

Puppy mills are something very different.

The problem is when the animals producing those puppies become a means to an end.

And veterinary care becomes an expense to minimize or avoid, not an essential part of responsible animal care.

When it comes to looking for your next four-legged family member, start your search at an animal shelter. Research your favorite breed and know how to recognize a suspicious situation.

If you are planning to purchase or adopt a puppy, you should be able to inspect the home or facility where the puppy was raised, and meet the puppyâs mother. Breeders who are unwilling or unable to allow this raise suspicions of unethical practice, and if you are concerned about a potential welfare issue, donât be tempted to buy a puppy to ârescueâ it â this simply finances the operation. Instead, contact your local animal control agency, humane society, sheriff, or police department.

When extreme conformation interferes with breathing and thermoregulation, when it increases the risk of difficult births and chronic airway problems, we need to consider whether breeding these dogs is the right thing to do. But if people will buy them, people will breed them.

Itâs up to us to look past the adorable face we saw on Instagram and ask:

And, as the horrific plight of these 48 dogs reminds us, where did they come from?

The problem is loving an appearance so much that we stop asking what that appearance means for the animal.

These dogs have been through a terrible situation, but now they have a chance.

They need veterinary care. Their nails need treatment, their skin and eyes need evaluation, their nutritional needs need to be addressed, and their other medical problems need to be properly investigated. Some require specialized treatment, while others are recovering in foster homes.

And hopefully, many of these dogs will eventually experience something that should have been completely ordinary from the beginning:

These dogs were not born to produce puppies. They were not born to be quiet. They were not born to look a certain way for someone else's profit.

For that reason, adoption should always be considered before buying a puppy.

There are so many wonderful dogs already waiting in shelters, foster homes, and recovering from neglect. Dogs that may not have the perfect face or pedigree but have an enormous capacity to love.

Please, before asking where to buy the puppy with the cutest face, ask who is already waiting for someone to choose them.

#7879. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Orphaned Kittens Are Suckling Each Other! (October 19, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

Kristin Davis filled a hollowed pumpkin with sunflowers. Experts explain how to make the centerpiece, from choosing the pumpkin to keeping the flowers fresh.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Charlotte York – ahem, I mean Kristin Davis of Sex and the City fame – recently showed off a Thanksgiving centerpiece that would look perfect on any table this fall.

Much like Catherine Zeta-Jones, Kristin has taken a DIY approach to her Thanksgiving decor, using homegrown pumpkins in a very different way to the usual tried-and-tested Halloween methods.

In the clip (which you can watch here), Kristin can be seen tucking a glass jar of sunflowers into a gutted pumpkin, transforming it into a vase. And, if you're interested in copying the look, I've consulted a few experts to help.

Shop A Cheat Version Of Kristin Davis's Pumpkin Vase:

If you want to steal Kristin Davis's Thanksgiving decor for yourself, the trick is to treat the pumpkin as a container, not a planter.

“Choose a firm, unblemished pumpkin, cut the top wide enough to fit a glass jar, and scoop the inside completely clean, because leftover pulp shortens the life of both the pumpkin and the flowers,” says Morgan Brooks, founder and editor of Plant Style Home.

Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, insists that you should “choose a pumpkin that’s flat with a large opening (slightly wider than it is tall, this will mean it’s lighter!)”.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The experts at Almondsbury Garden Centre insist that the jar element of Kristin Davis's Thanksgiving decor is non-negotiable. “Once hollowed out, place a glass jar or small watertight container inside to hold the water,” they say.

“This is important as pouring water directly into the pumpkin can cause it to soften and rot more quickly.” Brooks adds a practical bonus, saying “it lets you change the water every two days without disturbing the arrangement, which matters more for freshness than any floral preservative”.

Melam says most leaks and wilting come down to the same few things, all of which can be staved by the jar. “Dry off the pumpkin, choose a tight-fitting jar, remove all the leaves below the water line, and you will solve most of your problems.”

When it comes to filling your pumpkin vase, Melam has a tip for choosing your flowers, saying, “The most beautiful flower in the shop is the one with the least amount of time left in its life.” Look for buds that are just opening, because “when the bud first begins to open, there is still its prime to come.”

At home, Brooks says to “Cut the stems at a sharp angle, strip every leaf that would sit below the waterline, and condition them in warm water for an hour before arranging.”

Your next step is to build around your arrangement. “Sunflowers carry heavy heads on thick stems, so place them first as the structure of the arrangement and fill around them with smaller fall flowers and foliage,” says Brooks.

Reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, says the secret to recreating Kristin Davis's Thanksgiving decor is a tight palette. He says, “The key is to keep it thematic. Not just fall-themed, but dialed into a specific palette of colors that complement each other instead of standing out individually without coherence.” He does have one warning: “Fall colors are, to no fault of their own, awfully close to compost colors.”

Because sunflowers are so large, he suggests pairing them with “smaller blossoms, like alstroemeria, gypsophila, or small roses.” And don’t let the arrangement block the view across the table. “If in doubt, just keep it at 12 inches or shorter,” says Renwick.

The pumpkin fades first, so Melam advises making it ahead of time: “I’d suggest you put this together a day or two in advance and keep it in a cool place until needed.”

To keep costs down, raid your own garden. “If you have zinnias in your garden, your problems are solved,” says Renwick, who also recommends dahlias, marigolds, asters, and mums. Almondsbury suggests, “Using flowers and foliage from your own garden, such as autumn asters, dahlias and ornamental grasses, and adding just a couple of sunflowers for impact.”

When Thanksgiving is over, Melam says you can “Compost the pumpkin and save your favorite flowers.”

Kristin Davis’s centerpiece is appealing due to its simplicity; not everything needs to be super showy and over the top to steal the show at the Thanksgiving table.

#7877. Annoying Habits That Are Actually Cries for Help

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦

Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

Dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

The key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

Boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

Dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

Different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

Training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

For dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying issue rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

#7875. The Common Flea Pill Preventing New World Screwworm

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

For many cat parents, the brand Capstar might ring a bell. This small, fast-acting tablet has long been used to kill adult fleas on cats and dogs. Now, the active ingredient in Capstar, nitenpyram, is being given an important new role: treating and preventing New World screwworm.

On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA for nitenpyram tablets, allowing the common flea tablet to be used off-label for the prevention and treatment of New World screwworm infestations in cats, kittens, dogs, and puppies.

Why does this matter? Because until now, prevention was the missing piece when it came to drug options for dogs and cats. This new authorization helps fill that gap, giving veterinarians another tool in the toolbox while the larger fight against New World screwworm continues.

First things first: despite the rather dramatic name, New World screwworm is not a worm at all. It is a fly: Cochliomyia hominivorax. The âwormâ part of the name comes from the larvae, or maggot, of this fly. And unfortunately, this is one fly that definitely deserves our attention.

The trouble starts when a female fly finds a suitable place to lay her eggs, usually in or around a wound. She can also target other vulnerable areas, including the eyes, nose, mouth, and other mucous membranes. Once those eggs hatch, the larvae get to work, and this is where the screwworm becomes particularly nasty.

These aren't the disgusting but harmless little maggots that make themselves at home in overflowing trash cans or rotting food. Screwworm larvae feed on living tissue, burrowing deep into the affected area, feeding as they grow. Before long, a wound that looks small on the outside has become a much bigger problem underneath. An infestation can cause extensive tissue damage and, without prompt treatment, can even be life-threatening.

New World screwworm has been detected in the United States, while Mexico and other countries in the region continue to deal with the parasite. USDA is maintaining surveillance and response efforts, including in Texas, where âzones of infestationâ have been established.

The concern goes well beyond individual animals. Screwworm can have a serious economic impact on livestock production because affected animals may lose weight, require treatment and extra care, or die. During a 1976 outbreak in Texas, producers spent an estimated $132.1 million dealing with the pest, equivalent to about $740 million in 2024 dollars. More recently, the disruption to live cattle exports from Mexico has been estimated to have cost that country's livestock sector around $1.8 billion.

This is why so much effort is going into keeping this fly from spreading. This is about animal health, but it is also about protecting our entire food production system.

And no, the strategy is not simply âfind the bugs and squish them.â Controlling screwworm takes a much bigger effort. Authorities are using surveillance, movement controls, trapping, and other measures, along with one particularly interesting tool: releasing sterile flies.

The idea is surprisingly simple. Sterile male flies are released into affected areas, where they compete with fertile males for mates. When a sterile male mates with a female, she does not produce viable offspring. Over time, this can cripple the wild screwworm population.

The good news is that this isn't something every cat owner needs to panic about. Where a cat lives, where it travels, and whether it spends time in an area where screwworm is present all make a difference. For cats traveling to or returning from affected areas, it's worth being a little more careful.

With screwworm, the goal is to understand the risk before the exposure happens and, whenever possible, st ay one step ahead of the fly. When you consider that cats are experts at hiding things, including small wounds, a puncture, scratch, or other break in the skin can be easy to miss under all that fur, especially in an outdoor cat.

A wound can become an invitation for a female screwworm fly to lay her eggs, and the larvae that hatch will feed on living tissue. Cats infested with screwworm larvae have wounds that aren't healing normally, visible maggots, an unusual odor, or discharge. In any situation, these signs warrant veterinary attention. If you happen to live near or have traveled to an area where the New World screwworm has been detected, be sure to mention it to your vet.

Not necessarily. This does not mean Capstar should suddenly become part of every cat's routine parasite prevention. As a flea treatment, it is particularly effective at killing adult fleas quickly, but doesnât provide long-term flea control.

A cat living indoors in an area where screwworm isn't present is in a very different situation from a cat traveling to an affected region or spending time outdoors there. Your veterinarian can help you decide whether your cat's particular situation calls for the medication.

In the case of screwworm, Capstar is used according to the Emergency Use Authorization, not the FDA-approved standard use. There are specific instructions for when and how it should be given.

If you're traveling with your cat to an area where screwworm has been identified, or returning from one, talk with your veterinarian before you go. International travel can also come with health certificates, inspections, and other paperwork, and the requirements vary depending on the country you're entering or passing through. Some documents must be completed within a specific window before travel, so don't leave the paperwork until the last minute.

For most cats, New World screwworm is not something to worry about every day. But for cats living in or traveling to affected areas, knowing the risk, knowing that preventive options are available, and knowing what to look for can make a real difference. Itâs also great to know that those options include a product that has been safely used in cats for decades.

The takeaway isn't that every cat needs Capstar, but when a parasite like screwworm becomes a concern, having a preventive option available can make it easier to protect cats that are actually at risk.

And when a parasite feeds on living tissue, âbetter safe than sorryâ is a pretty good philosophy.

#7874. The Peaceful Second Amendment Revolution

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

How the right was restored from its nadir half a century ago

This speech was delivered during Wyoming Law Week at the University of Wyoming College of Law, October 13, 2026.

Ladies and gentlemen, cowboys and cowgirls, good evening.

The title of my presentation, "The Peaceful Second Amendment Revolution," is about a revolution in the original meaning of that word: a return to the original starting point, as when the earth completes a revolution around the sun.

The American Revolution began in that conservative sense. The Americans wanted the British to respect all their pre-existing rights, including the written right to arms from the 1689 English Bill of Rights.

Law Week is an appropriate time to reflect on the rule of law and the revolutionary role of lawyers, then and now.

Writing in 1789, after victory in the American Revolution, physician David Ramsay explained one reason for the Revolution: "The study of law was common and fashion­able." David Ramsay, 1 A History of the American Revolution 29 (Lester H. Cohen ed., Liberty Fund, 1990) (1789). According to Ramsay:

"No order of men has, in all ages, been more favourable to liberty, than lawyers. When they are not won over to the service of government, they are formidable adversaries to it. Professionally taught the rights of human nature, they keenly and quickly perceive every attack made upon them. While others judge of bad principles by the actual grievances they occasion, lawyers discover them at a distance, and trace future mischiefs from gilded innovations."

‍Ramsay pointed out that half of the First Continental Congress, in 1774, were lawyers.

"Bred in the habits of public speaking, they made a distinguished figure in the meetings of the people, and were particularly able to explain to them the tendency of the late acts of parlia­ment. Exerting their abilities and influence in the cause of their country, they were rewarded with its confidence."

We ought always feel gratitude to those lawyers, and other Americans, who defended and advanced natural rights during the American Revolution. Tonight is the story of how one of the rights which those lawyers and others had guaranteed in our Constitution was nearly obliterated during the last third of the twentieth century. And how the peaceful revolution that has restored the Second Amendment was the cooperative work of millions of Americans, especially lawyers, and among them, especially legal scholars.

Although the story does involve the recovery of the original meaning of Second Amendment, the story is also about living constitutionalism; the most important reason the right to keep and bear arms survived against the attempts to destroy it was that the right lives and thrives in the hearts and minds of the American people.

The U.S. Supreme Court decisions of District of Columbia v. Heller in 2008 and McDonald v. Chicago in 2010 were the opposite of cutting edge. Those decisions were lagging indicators. They were the long-term consequence of elections, of a generation of historical scholarship, and of the refusal of millions of ordinary people to accept that a right they had always exercised and cherished could be defined out of existence by unreasoned pronouncements.

During the nineteenth century, virtually all commentators and courts treated the right to keep and bear arms as a broad individual right, including for people not in the militia.

The most influential legal treatise of the early republic, St. George Tucker's American edition of Blackstone, described the Amendment as securing the rights of self-defense and resistance to tyranny.

Next came William Rawle's 1825 A View of the Constitution of the United States of America, which said that if either Congress or a state government, in "blind pursuit of inor­dinate power" should "attempt" "to disarm the people," "this amendment may be appealed to as a restraint on both."

The great Supreme Court Justice and prolific legal scholar Joseph Story wrote in 1840 that

"The right of the citizens to keep and bear arms has justly been considered, as the palladium of the liberties of a republic; since it offers a strong moral check against the usurpation and arbitrary power of rulers; and it will generally, even if these are successful in the first instance, enable the people to resist and triumph over them."

The preeminent constitutional writer of the latter 19th century was Michigan Supreme Court Chief Justice and Michigan Law School Dean Thomas Cooley. In 1880 he explained that "The right is general." "[I]f the right were limited to those enrolled," in the militia, "the purpose of this guaranty might be defeated altogether by the action or neglect to act of the government it was meant to hold in check."

Congress agreed. When the former slave states attempted to keep the freedmen in de facto servitude by enacting Black Codes that forbade the freedmen to possess arms, or required them to obtain a license, the Reconstruction Congress in 1866 overrode President Andrew Johnson's veto and passed the Second Freedmen's Bureau Bill, guaranteeing the "consti­tutional right to bear arms" as among the "immunities and rights" of Americans. The Civil Rights Act and the Fourteenth Amendment were passed with a similar and oft-expressed intent.

The theory that the right to arms was actually not a right made its first substantial appearance in a 1905 Kansas Supreme Court decision, Salina v. Blaksley. The case involved a municipal ordinance against carrying a firearm while intoxicated; the ordinance was easy to uphold based on precedents from other states. But the Kansas court aimed to use the case to destroy the right. Section 4 of the 1859 Kansas Bill of Rights declared "that the people have the right to bear arms for their defense and security." Yet the Kansas court claimed that this provision, in the state constitution Bill of Rights, merely affirmed the inherent power to state government to conduct military activities. The Kansas court also claimed that the federal Second Amendment had the same, empty meaning.

The Kansas court could not cite a single authority for its radical propositions. For example, a Massachusetts case had said that the state constitution right to arms is not violated by requiring a permit for large armed parades. The Kansas court pretended that the Massachusetts court had declared that there is no right to arms.

Based on how the U.S. Supreme Court had misinterpreted the Fourteenth Amendment in The Slaughterhouse Cases and U.S. v. Cruikshank in the 1870s, the Second Amendment, like most of the rest of the Bill of Rights, was not considered applicable to the States in the latter 19th and 20th centuries. State courts varied in how strictly they enforced their state constitution right to arms.

In 1934, Congress passed the first major federal gun control law, the National Firearms Act, which required a hefty $200 tax and registration for a small subset of arms, including machine guns and short-barreled shotguns. The Supreme Court said in U.S. v. Miller that the short-barreled shotgun owned by a bootlegger had not been shown to be the sort of arm useful to a militia, and it upheld the National Firearms Act on that narrow ground. Notably, the Court was very interested in Miller's weapon, and did not even mention that Miller while bootlegging was not actively serving in the Arkansas militia.

The Supreme Court's decision was consistent with the most restrictive line of state constitution cases from the 19th century, all of which came from States of the Confederacy: every individual citizen had the right to arms, but only for the types of arms used in "civilized warfare." For example, rifles, swords, or large handguns, but not pocket pistols.

The First Circuit, in the 1942 Cases v. United States, said it would not follow Miller any further than Miller's particular holding about the short-barreled shotgun. According to Cases, the Miller rule, if generalized, would protect far too many weapons.

That same year, the Third Circuit in U.S. v. Tot asserted that the Second Amendment "was not adopted with individual rights in mind," and further asserted that the Supreme Court had said so in Miller.

Congress did not think so. Shortly before U.S. entry in World War II, the U.S. Congress passed the Property Requisition Act, to allow the executive branch to seize, with full compensation, property needed for the national defense. Except for firearms. The federal government could not seize or register firearms possessed "by any individual for his personal protection or sport." The government could not "impair or infringe in any manner the right of any individual to keep and bear arms." The committee report explained that right to arms protections were "[i]n view of the fact that certain totalitarian and dictatorial nations are now engaged in the willful and wholesale destruction of personal rights and liberties."

But things changed drastically starting in the late 1960s. First, by then the original public meaning of much of the Bill of Rights and of the Fourteenth Amendment had been long forgotten. Many original source documents were not available in any practical sense to federal or state court libraries. For example, David Young' 1997 book The Origin of Second Amendment would compile hundreds of original documents about the right to arms from 1787 to 1792; as of the 1960s or 1970s, most of these documents existed in archives, and were waiting to be rediscovered by scholars and published in modern anthologies. But not yet.

Beginning in the mid-1960s, surging violent crime rates and race riots all over America terrified the public. In 1963, President Kennedy was assassinated by a communist using a mail-order rifle; then in April 1968 Martin Luther King was assassinated by a racist using a rifle; and then in June Senator Robert F. Kennedy was assassinated by an anti-Jewish Jordanian immigrant using a cheap imported handgun.

Connecticut Senator Thomas Dodd was Chairman of the Senate Subcommittee on Juvenile Delinquency and in the early 1960s he had been criticizing violence on television and cinema. But under pressure from Hollywood and from advertisers, Dodd had shifted his focus to guns, and in 1968, after the second Kennedy assassination, he was able to pass the Gun Control Act of 1968. As amended, it is still the major federal gun control law.

The Act banned mail-order gun sales, outlawed the import of inexpensive pistols, and imposed many other controls. But it did not fulfill the objectives of President Lyndon Johnson and other advocates for national gun licensing or national gun registration.

Most notably, from the viewpoint of the federal courts, the Act greatly expanded the categories of persons who were forbidden by federal law to possess a firearm or ammunition. Prosecutorial resources for such crimes were also greatly augmented.

Soon, the federal courts were hearing many cases from convicted felons, whose desperate public defenders were arguing that prohibiting a convicted violent felon from possessing a firearm violated the Second Amendment.

In 1973, the Office of Legal Counsel under President Nixon, who personally opposed all firearms ownership by citizens, wrote a formal opinion that there is no personal constitutional right under the Second Amendment to own or use a gun.

The federal judges appointed by Presidents Johnson and Nixon tended to be hostile to gun ownership. So rather than simply upholding bans on gun possession by convicted violent felons, many federal courts denied that there was an individual Second Amendment right. Instead, the right was said to a "collective" right that no individual could exercise. This is similar to "collective property" in communist dictatorships, where property supposedly belongs to all the people, but in fact only to the government.

Or the right was said to a "States' right," although nobody who said so could articulate what this right was. Or why the authors of the U.S. Constitution, who repeatedly used the word "State" or "States" to identify states' rights, had momentarily forgotten when they were writing the Second Amendment, and had written "the People" when they actually meant "the States."

The judicial opinions were typically terse and contemptuous, often consisting of string cites of post-1968 federal cases, all of which traced back to Tot or Cases. The opinions dared not quote the Supreme Court's words in Miller that in the Second Amendment's militia, "ordinarily when called for service these men were expected to appear bearing arms supplied by them­selves and of the kind in common use at the time."

The purpose of the nullificatory lower court opinions was not to describe what the Second Amendment was. Rather, the effort was to declare by ipse dixit that there was no individual right. The effort reached its zenith of absurdity in a 1975 report of the American Bar Association asserting, "It is doubtful that the founding fathers had any intent in mind with regard to [the] meaning of this amendment." Ben R. Miller, The Legal Basis for Firearms Controls, 100 Ann. Rep. A.B.A. 1050, 1052 (1975).

So according to the ABA, the Second Amendment was essentially similar to the Beatles song "I am the Walrus," for which John Lennon wrote nonsense lyrics to get even with people who overanalyzed Beatles songs.

Man, you should have seen them kicking Edgar Allan Poe.

In 1974, two national groups were formed in the District of Columbia to ban handguns, although they later expanded their objectives to include long guns. The National Coalition to Ban Handguns is now known as the Coalition to Stop Gun Violence. The other was the National Council to Control Handguns, which after several name changes is today known as Brady.

The leader of the latter group explained the strategy to The New Yorker in 1976: "The first problem is to slow down the increasing number of handguns being produced and sold in this country. The second problem is to get handguns registered." Finally, make "totally illegal" "the possession of all handguns and all handgun ammunition," except for the government and a few exceptions, such as licensed collectors.

Shortly after Congress granted the District of Columbia home rule, the District Council in 1975 took the initiative and banned handguns and forbade residents from keeping any firearm loaded and assembled for self-defense inside the home.

In 1976, Massachusetts put a handgun confiscation measure on the ballot. Although early polling was favorable, the measure lost, 69% to 31%. It even lost in Boston. Although the Boston police chief was a fervent advocate, the rest of law enforcement, including police unions and police chiefs, was almost unanimously opposed. They pointed out the ban would not affect criminals but would disarm law-abiding citizens, including off-duty police.

After the landslide defeat, an official with the League of Women Voters (which had vigorously supported the ban) said, "I think a lot of voters have that idea that this was designed to get guns away from the criminals. That's not the real purpose."

In the opinion of the gun confiscation movement, the American people are not capable of keeping firearms in their home without eventually harming themselves.

Morton Grove, Illinois, banned handguns in 1981, and during the next several years, Chicago and five more nearby suburbs followed suit. But the reaction across the rest of the country was a wave of state preemption laws. Legislatures decided that cities would not be allowed to outlaw firearms the state itself permitted. Within a few years, the possibility of municipal gun bans had been eliminated in most states.

Prohibitionists tried next in California in 1982, with a ballot initiative for a "handgun freeze." Unlike the Massachusetts measure, the California freeze would allow current owners to keep their handguns.

The California initiative was defeated by a vote of 63% to 37%. Opposition to the freeze brought so many additional voters to the polls that they even carried the Republican to a 1% victory for Governor.

In 1993-94, President Clinton was enthusiastically supporting gun control, and so the confiscation lobbies tried ballot initiatives in three left-leaning cities in Wisconsin, one of the few states without preemption. After confiscation was defeated in Milwaukee, Kenosha, and even in Madison, the backlash led to the enactment of Wisconsin preemption, and then to a state constitution right to arms adopted with 73% voter support.

Nationally, President Clinton worked tirelessly on gun control, passing a major anti-crime bill September 1994 that included a 10-year ban on the sale or manufacture of many semiautomatic firearms and on standard magazines over 10 rounds.

In November 1994, Democrats lost control of the U.S. House for the first time since 1953. President Clinton said, "The NRA is the reason the Republicans control the House." A Conversation with President Clinton, Cleveland Plain Dealer, Jan. 14, 1995, at 11B. Clinton also blamed the NRA for the 1993 defeat of New Jersey Governor James Florio, who had signed a similar ban.

At the state level, the 1994 elections led to tremendous changes in state gun laws. State after state enacted standardized, objective Shall Issue licensing for handgun carry permits; new or enhanced preemption laws to eliminate local gun control; instant checks to replace state-level waiting periods for handgun purchases; range protection bills to prevent noise nuisance suits against shooting ranges; and other right to arms measures.

In 1999, the murders of 12 students and one teacher at Columbine High School south of Denver reinvigorated the gun control movement. Indeed, in many states and in Congress, the immediate aftermath of a mass shooting is the only opportunity for antigun activists to win legislative victories. A few weeks after Columbine, Vice President Al Gore cast the tie-breaking vote in the U.S. Senate for an amendment to a juvenile crime bill that would have given the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives the administrative power to shut down any or all gun shows in the United States.

The 2000 presidential election promised to be the great showdown on gun control. Like the election of 1800 for the First Amendment (when the Sedition Act was being used to silence Republican opposition to the Federalists), the 2000 election would decide the fate of the Second Amendment.

In response to a letter from a concerned citizen, Clinton's Solicitor General Seth Waxman articulated the DOJ's position that "the Second Amendment does not extend an individual right to keep and bear arms." Quoting the citizen's letter, Waxman concurred that the government believes that it "could 'take guns away from the public,' and 'restrict ownership of rifles, pistols and shotguns from all people.'" The NRA put Waxman's "take guns" quote on billboards in swing states.

President Clinton later wrote that the NRA had been the reason that his Vice-President Al Gore lost five swing states in the Southeast, and hence the election.

The Justice Department under President George W. Bush withdrew the old Nixon administration opinion. In its place came an Office of Legal Counsel opinion over 100 pages, affirming the individual right.

Bush won re-election by a close margin in 2004, contrasting his support of gun rights with Massachusetts Senator John Kerry, an ardent gun control advocate. That election would made the difference in the 5-4 decision in District of Columbia v. Heller, decided at the end of President Bush's second term in 2008. President Bush had nominated John Roberts and Samuel Alito; whereas the Democratic shortlist included former Solicitors General Seth Waxman and Walter Dellinger and D.C. Circuit Judges David Tatel and Merrick Garland, all of whom defended handgun bans.

State Constitution ballot measures are the highest possible means by which the people can express their views on what ought to be a right. Since 1978, 17 states by vote of the people have added or strengthened state constitution right-to-arms provisions. (In 2026, Arkansas.) Not a single proposed amendment to fortify the right has ever been defeated at the ballot box.

Starting in the 1970s, pollsters began asking Americans if they believed they had a constitutional right to arms, and large majorities always said yes.

But not the large majority of the scholarly and legal elites, starting in the 1960s. To many of them, the notion that an ordinary American had a right to own a firearm and use it for self-defense was unbearable. The idea could not even be considered.

Those who did dare consider it tended to be practicing lawyers, whose professional livelihood did not depend on the approval of law professors. Starting in the 1970s, Virginia attorney Stephen Halbrook did more than anyone else to found the field of firearms law. His career record in U.S. Supreme Court merits cases is five wins and zero loses, including Printz v. United States in 1997, one of the most important modern federalism decisions, and NRA v. Oak Park, the companion case to McDonald v. Chicago in 2010, making he Second Amendment enforceable against the States via the Fourteenth Amendment.

Author of the Thomson West treatise on Firearms Law, Halbrook has been a prolific author of law journal articles and books, especially on the history of the right to arms.

He has taken full advantage of the fact that, because every law school has at least one law review, law has many more scholarly journals than do most other disciplines, so there is much more room for publication of articles that do not conform to the conventional wisdom of the moment.

Next to Halbrook, the lawyer who did the most in the long term for the restoration of the Second Amendment was the late Don Kates. As a Yale Law Student, Kates had volunteered for the 1964 Freedom Summer, to provide support for rural Black Mississippians to register to vote. In late June, three civil rights workers were murdered.

Kates adopted the longstanding practices of the Black and White civil rights workers who lived in the South fulltime: carrying firearms for protection against the Ku Klux Klan and other violent white supremacists who were tacitly supported by local law enforcement. After graduation, Kates went to work for California Rural Legal Assistance, and was soon named poverty lawyer of the year by the National Legal Aid and Defender Association.

Kates began to specialize in firearms law, and he too became a prolific scholar. In 1983, the Michigan Law Review, including me as a student citechecker, published Kates' article "Handgun Prohibition and the Original Meaning of the Second Amendment."

The Kates article in the Michigan Law Review was the first article about the Second Amendment  that had appeared in what was then a top-5 law review since the early 20th century. Professor William Van Alstyne, who was an eminent constitutional law textbook author and very liberal, later recounted that "this pipsqueak Kates," who was not a law professor, had convinced many of the leading constitutional law professors that the Second Amendment really was an individual right.

But none dared express that idea in print. That is why Sanford Levinson, also a very eminent and very liberal constitutional law professor, titled his 1989 essay in the Yale Law Journal "The Embarrassing Second Amendment." He wrote:

"I cannot help but suspect that the best explanation for the absence of the Second Amendment from the legal consciousness of the elite bar, including that component found in the legal academy, is derived from a mixture of sheer opposition to the idea of private ownership of guns and the perhaps subconscious fear that altogether plausible, perhaps even 'winning,' interpretations of the Second Amendment would present real hurdles to those of us supporting prohibitory regulation."

Reassured by Levinson's grant of respectability and permission, many law scholars began to explore the unknown-to-them legal history of the Second Amendment. The large majority found the Second Amendment to guarantee a normal individual right. Other explorers  agreed that the Second Amendment was meant to be an individual right, but argued that the right no longer existed because conditions had changed; for example, the American people today are no longer virtuous and unified, as they supposedly were in 1791.

Besides Halbrook and Kates, there were many other lawyers and professors who played a role, including Arizona attorney David Hardy since 1974.

Federal courts often move slowly. It took until 2001 for a modern federal circuit panel, the Fifth Circuit in United States v. Emerson, to hold that the Second Amendment is an individual right.

The next Circuit to come around was the D.C. Circuit in 2007, whose decision striking the D.C. handgun ban would be affirmed by the Supreme Court the next year in Heller.

By the time Heller was being briefed in December 2007, even the gun ban groups had given up on the "collective right" theory that had once been hegemonic in elite circles. Only one amicus brief in support of the D.C. ban argued for the collective right theory at length, and it came from President Clinton's former Attorney General Janet Reno and some other former officials.

The Supreme Court in Heller ruled unanimously that the Second Amendment was an individual right. Justice Stevens' dissent expressly rejected the collective right. Instead, he described the Second Amendment as a narrow individual right that could only be asserted by individuals who were upholding a state's interest in its militia. That particular theory had been invented in 1989 by gun control attorney Dennis Henigan, who had studied the issue in enough depth to realize that the negation of an individual Second Amendment right was untenable.

The problem for Henigan and other supporters of the DC handgun ban was that the text of the Second Amendment guaranteed "the right of the People," and not "the right only of people actively serving in the militia." Since the 1990s, scholars had been calling the normal individual right for the general public "the standard model." The standard model was standard because it had been the standard model throughout the first century of the Second Amendment.

The standard model never forbade all gun control. In constitutional litigation over the Second Amendment or other liberties safeguarded by the Bill of Rights, the standard result is that the civil rights advocates and opponents each win sometimes and lose sometimes.

That is where the Second Amendment is today; as in the Early Republic and thereafter, there will always be disputes about what it means for the right to be "infringed." Many gun controls are not even challenged, and when there are challenges, the government usually wins. But not always, because the Second Amendment is today recognized as a meaningful and enforceable constitutional right that safeguards  natural right.

In the United States of America, the Rule of Law includes the government obeying the Constitution; the freedom of speech, including academic speech; free elections; and the leading role of liberty-minded lawyers in public life. All of these combined the rescue a fundamental right from a nadir half a century ago. The revolutionary restoration of the right to arms was accomplished peacefully, thanks to and because of the Rule of Law. This week, let us celebrate the Rule of Law, and let each of us honor it with our conduct every day of the year.

Further discussion, including citations, can be found in Kopel, The Great Gun Control War of the 20th Century--and its Lessons for Today, 39 Fordham Urban Law Journal 1257 (2012); and The Right to Arms in the Living Constitution, 2010 Cardozo Law Review de Novo 99.

David Kopel is research director at the Independence Institute.

Fall yard cleanups tend to focus on weather-beaten perennials and messy plant skeletons lingering in beds and borders – but don’t neglect your backyard’s biggest plant!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For homeowners, November represents the last opportunity to prepare your backyard’s largest living feature for the rigors of winter. Yes, I’m talking about your lawn. The weather can change on a dime, and if you’re not careful, it can leave its mark all over your lawn. Depending on where you live, one week can mark the difference between lush grass and frozen turf.

Thankfully, these lawn care essentials are neither grueling nor time-consuming. Do these simple jobs now, and they will save you trouble and expense later. They will help to protect your turf over winter and give it the healthiest start next spring. From what to do with your mower to when to apply that last round of fertilizer, these pivotal lawn care tasks can help with any shape or size.

These tips can also help you whether you have warm or cool-season grasses to deal with. You just need to adapt the approach depending on which type you are growing. Cool-season grasses like Kentucky bluegrass, fescue, and perennial ryegrass remain semi-active in November. But warm-season varieties such as Bermudagrass, Zoysia, and St Augustine are approaching dormancy. Here are the 6 key tasks you need to check off before the first true hard freeze locks your soil for the season.

When freezing temperatures arrive, your lawn’s soil moisture solidifies, expanding underground and turning grass blades brittle. In severe cold snaps, winds can wick moisture, inducing winterkill. Conversely, heavy snow falling on debris-laden turf can create the stagnant breeding grounds favored by snow mold fungi. Keep your USDA hardiness zone and regional weather in mind with these tips, but try to think one step ahead of the worst-case scenario so you don’t get caught out.

Before diving into these tasks, it’s important to check your soil temperature. Turf reacts to ground conditions, with root growth in cool-season lawns tapering off once soil temperatures plunge below 45°F (7°C). Second, verify that your mower blades are sharp. Dull mower blades can shred dormant grass tips, leaving wounds that turn brown, lose moisture, and invite cold-weather fungal pathogens. If you haven’t got one, the Sharpal 103N All-In-One Lawn Mower Blade Sharpener from Amazon is a great-value gadget for restoring razor-sharp cutting edges.

Spending just an hour or so on late-fall lawn preparation right now will really pay off when the warm spring weather returns. It also gives your grass all the help it needs to get through the sleet, wind, frost and snow that could be waiting just round the corner. Whatever your growing zone and grass species, here’s what you need to do to get your grass fully winter-ready!

Allowing heavy leaves to carpet your turf over winter is one of the quickest ways to ruin a healthy sward. This is a vital task for all types of turf, whether your grass is going dormant for the winter or not. For grass that is still growing, thick layers of leaves block sunlight and energy production. For grasses in any stage of growth or dormancy, leaves can trap moisture, restrict airflow, and encourage disease. Left unchecked, smothering leaves will suffocate entire sections of turf, leaving bare, dead zones by spring.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Your removal strategy should match the volume of fallen leaf cover. For light to moderate leaf scatter, use a mulching mower and let the nutrients fall naturally into the ground. However, if your yard is buried under dense, wet blankets from mature oaks or maples, rake or blow them off immediately. If you’re after a good rake, the True Temper Clog-Free 24-inch Poly Leaf Rake from Walmart is durable and reliable and won’t tear at late-season turf. Collect the leaves for rich leaf mold or vegetable garden mulch. Focus extra attention on perimeter fence lines and low dips in the lawn, where fall winds can quickly create suffocating drifts.

Timing your final mow comes down to knowing your grass type, and considering the weather. In northern regions, cool-season grasses (fescues, bluegrass, ryegrass) continue growing until ambient soil temperatures consistently sit below 40°F (4°C). So they could still be growing in November if the weather is mild, but plan for a last cut soon. In the south, warm-season lawns (Bermuda, St. Augustine, Zoysia) have ceased upward growth and could be dormant already, so your last cut may already have happened.

When making a final cut, aim for a medium length. Cutting grass too short will leave the lawn more vulnerable to stress over winter, exposing tender root crowns to frost heaving and biting winds. Conversely, leaving turf overly tall causes long blades to fold over under heavy snow or winter rain, forming dense mats that trap moisture and increase the risk of disease. Aim for a final height of 2-2.5 inches (5-6cm) for cool-season lawns, and 2 inches (5cm) for warm-season lawns.

Once complete, hose down the underside of the mower deck, empty the fuel tank or run the carburetor dry, and store your mower away clean. Buy Sta-Bil Storage Fuel Stabilizer Fluid from The Home Depot to help keep leftover fuel fresh while mowers are stored in winter and give effortless startups next spring.

Late-fall lawn fertilization can be either beneficial or destructive, depending on the species of grass you cultivate. For cool-season turf, late fall is often considered the most important feeding of the year. Cool-season roots remain active, absorbing nitrogen and potassium. So this last infusion of nutrients supports strong root development and helps encourage early spring green-up and drought resistance. Buy Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard from Lowe’s for a slow-release boost to cool-season roots.

Timing depends on location. In some areas, November may be too late for a last application. Apply fertilizer only while the grass is still green and before the ground freezes solid. If you’re unsure, contact your local extension office for guidance. Meanwhile, warm-season grasses should not be fed in November. They are entering dormancy or are already dormant. Nutrients added now could trigger new growth that have zero cold tolerance, leaving the turf vulnerable to winterkill during sudden freezes. Wait until spring to feed your warm-season turf.

Cooler weather and shorter daylight hours reduce your lawn’s evaporation rates. Continuing to run summer lawn watering schedules through November wastes water and runs the risk of waterlogging. If your cool-season turf is green and receiving less than an inch of natural rainfall per week, you only need to provide occasional deep waterings. Irrigate only when the top two inches (2cm) of soil feel dry to the touch, and irrigate during morning hours so grass blades dry before nightfall.

Do think about winterization with watering, too. Trapped water in underground pipes, sprinkler bodies, and backflow preventers expands upon freezing, cracking brass valves and rupturing poly lines. Turn off the main water shutoff valve, deactivate the controller, and blow out the lines using a commercial air compressor, or open manual drain valves. Disconnect, drain, and coil all garden hoses, storing them indoors. Leaving a pressurized hose attached to an outdoor spigot traps water inside the sillcock, leading to burst interior pipes during winter freezes.

You can get Frost King FC1 Foam Faucet Covers from Walmart in double packs. Durable, weather-sealed expanded polystyrene shells with rubber cinch ties that insulate exterior spigots against freeze damage.

Spotting thin, bare patches in your lawn during November is frustrating, but rushing out with a bag of standard seed and fertilizer is usually a waste of time and money. Across most northern and transitional zones, soil temperatures have dropped below the 50-55°F (10-13°C) threshold required for grass seed germination. Seed spread now will absorb moisture, fail to sprout, rot in cold mud, or be devoured by birds. Similarly, warm-season varieties cannot establish from seed in late fall.

Use November to diagnose and prep. Determine why the patch developed: is it compacted soil from a high-traffic shortcut, poor drainage, pet urine, or heavy tree shade? Aerate the bald soil with a hand cultivator, incorporate a light dusting of compost, and make a plan for early spring overseeding. If you live in an area with reliable, long-lasting winter snow cover, you can experiment with dormant seeding. Spread cool-season seed over the prepped soil just before the first big snowfall. The seed will remain dormant over winter, and the freeze-thaw cycles work the seeds into the dirt for uniform germination during the first warm days of March.

Grass enters a vulnerable state in dormancy, and plants lose their natural elasticity. Walking, driving, or playing on frosted or frozen turf fractures brittle leaf blades and crushes delicate crowns. This creates winter lawn damage like marks and ruts that will not heal until active growth resumes in spring. Plan to keep people and pets off the grass for the next few months. Move playsets and heavy equipment off the lawn.

Another source of damage in winter is rock salt on nearby driveways and sidewalks. This can run off into lawn edges, drawing moisture away from grass roots and creating toxic soil conditions. So transition to plant-safe de-icing compounds. You can buy Natural Alternative Ice Melt from Amazon, which is safer for lawns and pet paws. Finally, avoid late-season core aeration or power dethatching, which can do more harm than good as grass prepares for winter.

Not every November lawn task will be required for every yard. It comes down to understanding your grass type, watching the weather forecast, and focusing on clearing leaves, timing a final cut, managing water correctly, and limiting traffic over vulnerable winter grass. Tackle these chores now to protect your grass over winter and to give it the best chance at a healthy, strong start next spring.

If you’re worried that erotica is “beneath you,” then fear not. First, on all these sites, you’re free to publish under a pen name. Furthermore, you might be surprised to know that erotica isn’t the low-grade smut of the past. Even vampire-enthusiast and best-selling author Anne Rice has written and published highly popular erotica. Her Sleeping Beauty series is a masterclass in sexy retellings of classic fairytales that we highly recommend.

With that in mind, we’ve put together some basic writing tips:

How do you know if what you write is worth publishing? If it takes your breath away or leaves you squirming in your seat, there’s a good chance that it’ll do the same for someone else. Share the goods.
