#7797. The 27 Best Gifts for DIYers and Tool Lovers: Tools, Accessories, Workwear, and More

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 7, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Selecting the right gift for a handy person can be tricky. Tinkerers and tool lovers tend to have an established set of go-tos for most jobs, or at least a preferred line of equipment, like Ryobi or Ego Power+ Tools. Lucky for you, we’ve been looking at tools all year long—including several new releases that we’ve named 2026 Tools of the Year. Using all that research and our team’s personal wish lists, we pulled together this holiday gift guide for tool lovers.

➜ Plus: Don’t miss our favorite multitools to give as gifts.

Whether you’re looking for one of the best power tool sets to surprise a significant other or trying to find a quality tool box for a beginner DIYer, this guide has a wide variety of the best tool gifts available. Find flashlights, pocket knives, socket sets, and more in this holiday guide to the top tool gifts and satisfy the tool aficionado in your life.

A good tool chest does more than hold tools, and the Husky 9-Drawer Mobile Workbench Cabinet proves it. Our pick for best overall in our best tool chests guide, it pairs nine soft-close drawers with a solid wood worktop and a built-in power strip with six outlets and two USB ports, allowing your garage to double as a charging station. Sturdy casters roll it wherever you need to work, and its all-welded steel body is built for years of heavy use.

What our tester says: “We’ve had this tool chest for several years, and it stores the majority of our tools, charges all our lawn care and vacuum batteries, and serves as a regular work surface in our garage. We haven’t had a single issue with it since we got it.” —Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Husky 9-drawer tool chest at The Home Depot.

Recently named a workwear Tool of the Year, these Red Wing IronFlex safety-toe boots deliver the perfect blend of comfort and protection in demanding conditions, right out of the box. Built with a non-metallic safety toe, waterproof lining, and slip-resistant outsole, they meet ASTM standards for safety and electrical hazard protection. The BOA lace system micro-adjusts for a precision fit, and the 6-inch uppers provide excellent ankle stability. Thanks to a dual-construction design (a welted heel for ground stability with a flexible cemented forefoot), they even offer just enough give for tasks where you need to stoop or kneel.

What our tester says: “My favorite thing about these boots was how comfortable they were. They didn’t need any break-in time, and the uppers gave me the perfect amount of ankle support.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Red Wing safety-toe boots at Red Wing.

For the DIYer or hobbyist who loves a good project, the Dremel 4300 is a corded rotary tool with a 1.8-amp motor and a speed range of 5,000 to 35,000 RPM. As the overall award winner in our best rotary tools guide, it barely slowed down when we ran it through thick steel, cutting faster than any other model we tested. The kit also comes with a detachable work light, a universal chuck, and a set of accessories we rated the best of the group, including EZ Lock cut-off wheels that swap on and off without a tool. Grinding and sanding wheels and carving bits all fit in a hard case, so it makes an easy gift that arrives ready to use.

Read our full review: Dremel 4300-5/40 Rotary Tool Kit

What our tester says: “It’s hard to beat the sheer power of the 4300. I’ve used it for cutting, grinding, and drilling, and it’s never let me down.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Dremel rotary tool kit at The Home Depot, Amazon, or Lowe’s.

Plenty of home projects happen in dark corners, from inside cabinets to crawl spaces to the underside of a dashboard. The Bosch FL12 12V LED Work Light illuminates them all with up to 330 lumens and a wide flood beam. And since it sets down on any flat surface or mounts using two built-in magnets, a carabiner clip, a nail hook, or a tripod screw, it even allows you to keep both hands free when you’re hard at work. Since it’s sold as a tool only, it’s a smart gift for someone who already uses Bosch 12V batteries.

Get the Bosch work light (tool only) at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Acme Tools.

Hand-forged in the USA from high-carbon steel, the Warwood Tool Company Perfect Axe is a tried-and-true tool built to be used and kept for years. It weighs just 2.25 pounds and comes with a hickory handle in either 19 or 28 inches, plus a leather mask to protect the blade between jobs. It’s well suited to clearing brush, splitting firewood, or trail work, which makes it a great gift for anyone with a yard to tame or logs to split.

Get the Warwood Tool Company axe at Warwood Tool Company.

Looking for a gift for the tinkerer who already owns pretty much every full-size tool? The Hoto Snapboq mini tool kit could be it. With just one interchangeable motor base, it switches between a mini rotary tool, an electric screwdriver, and a detail sander, meaning the single kit covers carving, polishing, and assembling small electronics. It charges via USB-C, and variable speed settings provide the control fine work needs.

Read our full review: Hoto Snapbloq 3-in-1 Mini Power Tool Kit

Get the Hoto tool kit at Amazon (sold individually) or Hoto.

Anyone who’s done a big project using a manual staple gun knows how fast it can wear out your hand. The Milwaukee M12 Crown Stapler, our top cordless pick in our best staple guns guide, takes the strain out of upholstery, insulation, and carpet jobs without an air hose in sight. It runs on a compact 12-volt battery, fires ⅜-inch flat crown staples from ¼ inch to 9/16 inch, and offers an adjustable power dial with two firing modes, plus a dry-fire lockout that protects your work surface.

Get the Milwaukee staple gun (tool only) at The Home Depot, Ace Hardware, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Not only does this impressive oscillating tool run smoother than most, but it also comes with a built-in LED light and an ergonomic grip for long hours of work in dimly lit locations, making it one of the best oscillating tools on the market. This kit also comes with several blades, a sanding block, sandpaper, a depth gauge, and an accessory storage box.

What our tester says: “We tested the oscillating tool on both wood and sheet metal. Even though 13,000 OPM is the low end of its speed range, which is higher than some, the DeWalt still cut smoothly through sheet metal in our test, proving that successful metal cutting isn’t only about speed. At the top speed of 20,000 OPM, it sawed quickly through wood. It also excelled in sanding.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the DeWalt oscillating multi-tool kit at Amazon.

Shameless plug: You could always gift a dad cap (or a screen-printed t-shirt or even an embroidered packable jacket) with OG home improvement icon’s name proudly stitched or printed. We’re biased, of course, but we think it’s a perfect project ensemble.

DIYers often find that having a pocket knife on hand quickly cuts down on the project difficulty, whether it’s slicing through plastic straps or dealing with tricky packaging. With its slim, lightweight design, this reverse tanto blade knife from Benchmade is perfect for an EDC (everyday carry) knife, camping, and use in emergency kits. DIYers will come to rely on the durable, corrosion-resistant steel blade for a host of household jobs.

What our tester says: “I really liked the reverse tanto point because it places more strength behind the blade tip for piercing, even though the point is broader than many of the others we tested. It also leaves a nice amount of upward curve in the edge for efficient slicing action.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Milwaukee is known for making quality tools and tool accessories, and its 56-piece socket set doesn’t disappoint. The kit includes both SAE and metric socket fasteners in a variety of sizes and comes in a sturdy, lightweight plastic case. It features a ratchet, a joint socket, extension bars, and a range of standard sockets made of durable alloy steel with a powder-coated finish to help protect against rusting and corrosion.

What our tester says: “I liked the fact that these sockets have a four-sided shape versus a round shape, which prevents them from rolling away and allows use with a transitional monkey wrench or crescent wrench to create more torque.” —Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer

Equipped with 18 tools packed into a compact stainless steel body, the Leatherman Wave Plus earned the easy-access award in our best multi-tools guide. During testing, our favorites of the bunch were the smooth and serrated knife blades, which we could open with one hand and without having to unfold the main handles. Add in the spring-action scissors, replaceable wire cutters, wood saw, and bit drivers, and it has everything you need for quick household fixes and minor repairs on the go.

What our tester says: “As an avid DIYer, I own a lot of tools. So many that I often can’t find what I’m looking for when I need it. But the Leatherman Wave Plus is one tool that I always keep within reach. It has 18 tools—including pliers and screwdrivers, saws and scissors, wire cutters, files, a knife, and more—all housed in a compact, ultra-durable package. It’s useful for so many projects!” —Jenny Stanley, Executive Editor

Get the Leatherman multi-tool at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or REI.

The Bosch Self-Leveling Cross-Line Laser is a great gift for tool lovers who value precision. With its 50-foot range, IP55 dust and water resistance, and smart self-leveling pendulum system that ensures accuracy within 5/16 inch at 30 feet, this laser level delivers the reliability and durability that tool enthusiasts will appreciate.

Get the Bosch self-leveling laser at Amazon.

Make it easy to navigate around the house or a busy jobsite with this rolling tool box by Keter, the best bang for the buck pick in our guide to the best rolling tool boxes. It has a broad base to store larger power tools, like a drill, circular saw, or impact driver, as well as six removable bins that are designed for storing small parts, tools, and hardware. It also sits on a pair of heavy-duty wheels and has a telescoping handle for improved mobility.

What our tester says: “I found the Masterloader very easy to open with one hand, and the sliding storage provided all the access I could ask for. I also liked the smaller compartment for hand tools that’s separate from power tools and parts (each of which has its own section).” —Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

From plumbing to electrical and everything in between, pliers are a reliable tool to help tackle a range of household projects. This seven-piece WorkPro set, which won the best bang for the buck award in our pliers guide, includes plumber’s pliers for gripping wet fittings, linesman pliers for twisting wires, slip joint pliers to work on the car, needle-nose pliers to access fasteners in tight locations, and a set of diagonal pliers to cut through wire and lightweight metal with ease. Consider this set of heat-treated pliers for the DIYer on your list.

The attractive appearance of the Opinel No.08 pocket knife, the best pocket-size pick in our whittling knives guide, is further enhanced by the high-quality durability and cutting power of the carbon-steel blade. It has a hard, durable beechwood handle that looks and feels great, as well as a 3.28-inch flat blade with a gentle curve toward the tip. We also love that it features a built-in locking mechanism that keeps the blade in place no matter whether it’s open or closed.

What our tester says: “The hard carbon-steel blade is sturdy enough to cut through hardwoods and softwoods when carving or whittling.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Small enough to slip into a stocking or slide beneath a big bow, the WD-40 Precision Pen is perfect for adding a bit of lubricant exactly where it’s needed. But that precision doesn’t come from its overall size, it comes from the fine-point felt tip that applies a single drop without overspray. And with a rubberized grip for comfort and a leak-resistant cap for safe carrying, it’s just as easy to use as it is to toss in a pocket or toolbox.

Read our full review: WD-40 Precision Pen

Get the WD-40 pen (various pack sizes) at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Tractor Supply Co.

When the power goes out or a project calls for a wide swath of light, the Fenix PD36R V2.0 is up to the challenge. It earned best overall in our best flashlights guide thanks to a powerful 1,700 lumens and a beam that reaches over 400 yards, all packed into a pocket-friendly aluminum body. A side switch cycles through five brightness levels, the tail switch gives instant on and off, and USB-C charging means no hunting for batteries.

Get the Fenix flashlight at Amazon or Fenix.

Not every tool storage option needs to have a host of drawers, shelves, and compartments to keep tools organized. This simple yet effective tool organizer by Bucket Boss, winner of the most versatile award in our best tool box organizers guide, fits on most 5-gallon buckets to provide DIYers with tool hooks for hammers, drills, pry bars, and other larger tools. In addition, the tool organizer is made with tough, durable fabric so DIYers don’t need to worry about the pockets and pouches being cut or torn by sharp knives, screwdrivers, or other common tools.

What our tester says: “I’ve used a bucket to carry my tools for years, but never with an organizer. The Bucket Boss was much more durable than I expected and had more than enough pockets for all my stuff. It’s a major upgrade.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Bucket Boss tool organizer at Amazon.

This limited-edition advent calendar from Craftsman puts a practical twist on the annual holiday countdown. Instead of traditional chocolates, this useful gift hides a high-quality hand tool, bit, or socket behind each door so that when Christmas comes, the recipient has a complete tool set plus a durable storage case. Whether for someone new to DIY or homeownership or simply looking to add to their setup, it’s a fun way to outfit a workshop.

Get the Craftsman advent calendar (before it sells out) at Amazon, Lowe’s, and Ace Hardware.

Screwdrivers are one of the most common hand tools used by DIYers and pros, so when the holidays roll around, consider this Klein Tools seven-piece set of slotted and Phillips screwdrivers. These screwdrivers have nonslip cushioned grips designed for ease of use and comfort. Each screwdriver features heat-treated blades that have been chrome plated to improve durability and increase corrosion resistance, ensuring the screwdrivers last as long as possible with proper use and maintenance.

What our tester says: “The Klein Tools set offered the best fit into most screw heads and the most comfortable grip of all the models I tested.” —Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Klein Tools screwdriver set at Amazon.

Drills are frequently paired with screwdriver bits to loosen or secure fasteners for a variety of household jobs, but the main purpose of a drill is to create uniform holes. As our best bang for the buck winner in our best drill bits for metal guide, this set of high-speed steel (HSS) DeWalt drill bits ranges in size from 1/16 inch to ½ inch, giving DIYers plenty of sizing options to choose from. The split-point tip design reduces the risk of the drill bit jumping or walking during use, while the tapered web construction helps improve durability and resist breakage.

What our tester says: “This particular set was incredible when it came to drilling metal. They didn’t walk at all and cut long, continuous, spiraled shavings.” —Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

A well-known saying in woodworking and for DIY projects in general is “measure twice, cut once.” For the most accurate outcome, it’s important to have a quality measuring tape, like this one from Stanley, our pick for easiest to read in our best tape measures guide. It has large lettering and markings, including both imperial and metric measurements, which eliminates the need to convert plan measurements from one system to another. It can stretch up to 26 feet in length and features a built-in nail hook to make long measurements easier to tackle with only one person.

What our tester says: “In addition to accuracy, this tape measure felt good while working. Visually, the tape’s uncluttered appearance, large block markings, and matte finish made it easy to read.” —Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Stanley measuring tape at Amazon.

Cut or split wood, plastic, and steel with this Horusdy 16-piece punch and chisel set, which includes a chisel gauge, five pin punches, two center punches, five tape punches, and three cold chisels. This set is made of chrome-vanadium steel that has been heat-treated to increase the hardness and durability of the tools. DIYers can use the punches to remove pins and bushings, as well as drive fasteners such as nails or dowels. Then, when the project is finished, the tools can be packed away into the included pouch for easy storage.

Get the Horusdy punch and chisel set at Amazon.

The best seat-style winner in our best tool chests guide, the Wen Garage Glider GG1350 is a padded rolling stool plus tool chest that lets you sit through low-level garage projects instead of crouching. Three drawers, 16 storage slots, and two fold-down magnetic trays keep your nuts, bolts, and screws within reach, and the swivel casters allow you to glide across the floor with ease. And since its sturdy steel frame supports up to 350 pounds, it’s solid enough to accommodate most.

What our tester says: “We’ve gotten a ton of mileage out of this Wen tool box in the past couple of months. Storage is definitely limited, but if you set it up for a certain set of tasks, it’s a great small tool chest to have in your garage.” —Michelle Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Wen tool chest at The Home Depot, Amazon, Lowe’s, Walmart, Northern Tool + Equipment, or Wen.

Give the gift of easy tool storage and organization with this blue enamel Trusco tool box. It opens in two directions to reveal a large open base for hammers, screwdrivers, and other medium-size tools. The top tier of the tool box features 10 small storage compartments to keep screws, bolts, washers, and any other fasteners or accessories contained. Additionally, this tool box boasts a tough alloy steel construction and includes a hole that goes through both sides of the lid, allowing the user to add a lock for enhanced security.

What our tester says: “Compared with other boxes of its size, it’s made with much higher-quality metal, and the fit and finish were spot on.” —Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

Recognized in our best new workwear and safety gear of 2026 lineup, Ryobi’s magnetic headlamp offers hands-free illumination for jobsites, home repairs, and dark crawl spaces. Blasting up to 625 lumens across three brightness modes, this compact light features a clever detachable design with a strong magnetic base that mounts directly to metal studs, vehicle hoods, or pipes. Its IP54 water- and dust-resistant housing withstands harsh project conditions, while the removable, USB-C rechargeable battery delivers up to 16 hours of continuous runtime.

Get the Ryobi headlamp at The Home Depot.

#7796. 6 Native Alternatives to Butterfly Bush

Butterfly bush (Buddleja davidii, Zones 5–9) might seem like an easy choice for a pollinator bed, given the name, but is it the right shrub for your garden? There are a couple of reasons you might want to think twice and consider native butterfly bush alternatives instead.

Originally from Asia, butterfly bush is a prolific bloomer that attracts pollinators like no tomorrow. Unfortunately, it is also a prolific seeder, easily spreading past its intended area and potentially outcompeting other plants. Even after the shrub is removed, its seeds can remain viable in the soil for years until conditions are favorable for germination.

Butterfly bush is listed as an invasive plant by several state and regional invasive-plant organizations across the Southeast. Although some cultivars on the market are advertised as sterile or seedless, their fertility varies, and some can still produce small amounts of viable seed. While low-fertility cultivars can reduce the risk of spreading, butterfly bush also lacks an important benefit of many native plants: It does not serve as a host plant for native butterfly caterpillars.

The good news is that if you’re open to planting butterfly bush alternatives, there are plenty of beautiful flowering shrubs native to the Southeast that have both high visual appeal and benefits for native pollinators, including butterflies. Many also provide food and habitat beyond their flowering season. Here are just a few to get started:

Blooming in late spring to early summer, false indigo bush produces distinctive spikes of purple flowers that attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. A wonderful nectar source for long-tongued pollinators and a host plant for several butterflies, including the silver-spotted skipper and gray hairstreak, it offers benefits besides its gorgeous blooms. Its tolerance of a range of moisture conditions makes it a versatile option for sunny garden spaces.

Virginia sweetspire produces fragrant white flower spikes in late spring, followed by colorful foliage in fall. Its adaptability to moist soils makes it an especially useful shrub for rain gardens and other sites where drainage can be a challenge. A nectar source for many bees and butterflies, it is also reported as a host plant for the American holly azure butterfly in the coastal Southeast.

Its fragrant flowers attract butterflies, hummingbirds, and long-tongued bees. Blooming in late summer, when some other shrubs have finished flowering, summersweet offers an additional nectar source later in the growing season. Summersweet is also worth thinking about for gardens with consistently moist soil. Although it tolerates full sun, it generally needs more moisture in sunnier locations.

This deciduous native azalea brings soft pink to white flowers to woodland gardens in mid-spring, often before its foliage has fully emerged. An excellent nectar source for many pollinators, including hummingbirds and butterflies, pinxterbloom azalea is particularly well suited to partially shaded garden beds with acidic soil.

Spicebush blooms in early spring, producing small yellow flowers before its leaves emerge. Its early flowers also provide nectar for pollinators, while the bright red fall fruits on female plants, when a male plant is nearby for pollination, offer food for birds. A host plant for the spicebush swallowtail, this native shrub also brings pretty yellow foliage to the fall landscape.

Flame azalea earns its name from its showy flowers, which bloom in shades of yellow, orange, and red from late spring to early summer. A terrific general nectar source for many pollinators, particularly butterflies, this deciduous shrub adds striking seasonal color to woodland gardens and other partially shaded spaces.

If you’re only interested in the “butterfly” aspect of butterfly bush and not the “bush” aspect, choosing a great plant becomes even easier. There is an entire world of pollinator plants to explore, from host plants for the Southeast to nectar-rich native perennials and annuals. By incorporating both nectar plants for adults and host plants for caterpillars, you can create a garden that supports butterflies throughout their life cycle.

#7795. Timber Stoves Scout Review: Wood-Fueled Warmth From a Tabletop Heater

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 7, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

My family spends a lot of time on our deck, and even when fall evenings start getting chilly, we still find ourselves wanting to be out there. To extend our outdoor living window, we’ve traditionally kept a basket of blankets available by the door and a stack of wood ready by the fire pit. But since building a fire isn’t always convenient, and huddling under a throw isn’t always sufficient, it’s not long before we’re back inside—enjoying our gas fireplace and worrying about the added energy cost only after the bill arrives.

Once we got it set up, Timber Stoves’ Scout tabletop pellet heater provided the perfect solution to our cold-weather woes. After spending many an evening over the last month enjoying eye-level fires that start in just a few seconds, here’s what we love about the unit and what you deserve a warning on before you buy your own.

Bottom line: The Timber Stoves Scout is a stylish, effective solution for outdoor warmth, offering ease of use and maintenance despite initial setup challenges.

Before we started testing the Scout, we definitely had our reservations. In a home with two high-energy dogs and a revolving door of teenagers, was it even safe to have a wood pellet stove on our picnic table? Then there was assembly, which was challenging at first. The instructions weren’t super clear, so we struggled to get the chimney to fit over the main chamber. We ended up using a flat-head screwdriver to nudge open the gap that runs the length of the chimney, and that provided the fraction of an inch it needed to slide on. We also weren’t sure whether to insert the self-tapping screws to keep everything connected (the instructions said yes, but an online video we found implied no—we went with yes). Even getting the pellets to light took a few tries, but once we added a couple of small pieces off some GreenSpark fire starters we had, they took right off.

The good news is that once we got that first fire lit, our worries were a thing of the past. The Scout has an absolutely charming aesthetic, and we quickly fell in love with its functionality as well. The viewing window is perfect for watching your own tiny fire while you share a meal or play a game, and once it’s cranking, it puts out impressive warmth over about a 5-foot radius. We actually got too hot the first night we used it (early evening temps were still in the low 60s), but all we had to do was stop adding pellets from the hopper, and it slowly died down on its own.

Beyond its impressive heat, the Scout tabletop pellet heater features a rugged design that’s clearly built to last. While we weren’t sure it would be safe to have a tall wood pellet stove up off the ground, the weighted base has kept it rock-solid and stable no matter how many times our dogs have crashed into the table. I definitely wouldn’t leave small children unsupervised around an appliance like this, but that’s standard for any fireplace or fire pit.

Upkeep has been a pleasant surprise as well. The dedicated ash collection tray makes cleanup quick and easy—you just dump the cooled ash between uses to keep air flowing freely through the chamber and add fresh pellets to the hopper. After enjoying at least a dozen fires over the past few weeks, the stainless steel body has taken on a pretty purple-and-brown patina in many places, and I’ve simply wiped off any soot that’s collected inside the viewing window with a dry paper towel. All this to say, if I had to assemble it all over again to get to where I am today, I’d do it in a heartbeat.

The holiday season brings warmth, magic, and, often, a welcome touch of festive cheer to our homes, but for those navigating small floor plans or packed closets, the aftermath can quickly turn into a post-holiday headache. Finding room for bulky holiday decorations can quickly take the joy out of this time of year. Fortunately, you can find ways to set the scene in a way that doesn’t require taking up too much of your precious storage space. From collapsible, fold-flat Christmas trees and re-plantable living trees to accents straight from your backyard or the grocery store, there are plenty of clever ways to celebrate big without cluttering your home.

One way to save space after the holiday is to plant your tree in your own backyard. By choosing a living Christmas tree, you’ll save space, reduce waste, and build memories that last for years to come. A living Christmas tree is sold with its roots still attached, often called a “balled and burlapped” tree. Not only will a living tree fill your home with a fresh pine scent, but replanting it provides environmental benefits, such as minimizing waste, reducing deforestation, providing wildlife habitat, and sequestering carbon. You’ll be able to extend your holiday joy by incorporating replanting the tree as part of your celebration with friends and family, and you’ll be able to enjoy it throughout the year. Look for a living Christmas tree at nurseries, garden centers, online retailers like Lynch Creek Farm and Trees.com, and specialized tree farms.

This classic evergreen makes an ideal Christmas tree—and it can be planted in your yard after the holiday.

Minimize how much space you need to store holiday decorations by purchasing some that inflate or pop up. This Pop Up Christmas Tree, for example, is a smart choice. No assembly is necessary, and it comes fully decorated with Christmas balls, ribbons, bows, and lights already in place. The stand collapses and the tree folds flat, so you can easily tuck it away once the holiday ends. You can also look for inflatables like trees, gift boxes, and snowmen that can be used inside or outside. Once deflated, they’ll be easier to store.

Tapping into nature is one of the easiest ways to decorate for the holidays without accumulating endless bins of off-season storage. By foraging organic materials right from your own yard or neighborhood, you can create a naturally elegant scene. Beyond being completely free and eco-friendly, natural décor easily transitions across seasons or can be safely returned to the earth once the festivities end by adding items to a compost bin, shredding branches into garden mulch, using twigs to kindle a fire in your fireplace or fire pit, creating winter backyard shelters for birds, or setting them out for municipal tree recycling.

Check out these sample natural holiday decorations:

Food can double as holiday décor, from ornaments to a table runner, without requiring any storage space once your guests have left. Either the decor items will get eaten, or you can place them in a compost bin. Here are some ideas for crafting gorgeous, aromatic pieces using simple grocery store items:

Investing in multipurpose décor is the ultimate strategy for keeping your home festive without adding post-holiday clutter to your storage space. By selecting items that easily transition into everyday accent pieces, you can maintain a warm, welcoming vibe long after the holiday season comes to an end.

#7793. Spring Returns to Ezequiel’s Cottage Garden in Argentina

While many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December. Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another update as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

Plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

Thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a big hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

Purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

This massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

Another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something new to discover just about everywhere!

Thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

#7791. How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

If you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

As a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell

Successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

Containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

It’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more quickly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

One advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

Because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

Mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

Use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

The ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the big-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

We can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

Not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

Are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

When composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

While incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also important to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

Sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

And don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

By definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

Don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a new life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you plan to harvest from them.

One of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

Some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you plan to leave them in place for a second season.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

Another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

Lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

Vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

Alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

And there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

They also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a new focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

In the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

#7789. The President Nominates Circuit Judges, Not Senators

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state.

There has been a momentous shift in the relationship between the President and the Senate, and most people have missed it.

Let's start with the Eighth Circuit. The Trump Administration interviewed Justice Cody Hiland, but determined he was not up to the task of being a circuit judge, so they offered him a federal district court seat as a consolation prize. Hiland shot back at the White House Counsel and refused the seat. He even wanted to rub it in Trump's face. The White House made a stellar nomination with Judge Lee Rudofsky. Hiland then told an entire room of law students about his experience as a lesson that should be learned. But Hiland had a friend in a high place. Senator Boozman of Arkansas lobbied Senator Tillis of North Carolina and Senator Cornyn of Texas to block Judge Rudofsky.

Apparently there were some discussions between the President and Boozman, and the President folded. Maybe Trump determined that he needed as many judges confirmed before January, so the identity of the judge didn't matter. Maybe Trump didn't want to create more problems with his caucus. Maybe Trump just didn't care. Who knows? Trump withdrew Rudofsky and nominated Hiland. There is no guarantee that Hiland gets a hearing and makes it through the process. We are so late in the game. And frankly, I wouldn't blame some of the other conservative senators from the Eighth Circuit for putting Hiland through the paces at the hearing. It's not clear to me he'll be able to answer all the questions. But regardless of what happens, Senator Boozman won and President Trump lost.

Now, onto my home, the Fifth Circuit. It is painfully clear there was some sort of deal between Judge Southwick and Senator Wicker. In no universe would the White House have picked Todd Butler without that deal. I've yet to hear anyone provide me a single shred of evidence that he is conservative beyond saying "All southern lawyers are conservative. Plus he's a Christian." What about Nathan Johnson and James Talarico? Moreover, Southwick announced on September 29 that he would take Senior Status, making it virtually impossible for another nominee to be selected.

Yesterday, I watched Butler's confirmation hearing with interest. He received a few softballs from Senator Grassley, a very warm welcome from Senator Kennedy, and some surprisingly nice questions from Senator Booker about representing police officers. Butler did not seem to understand departmentalism and mis-cited Marbury v. Madison. His answers were not particularly articulate--roughly on par with his oral argument before the Supreme Court. There was no depth or curiosity conveyed.  I actually think Butler tripped up on Senator Blumenthal's questions about January 6 and the election, but it didn't matter. He sailed through. Members of the conservative legal movement have raised doubts about Butler. But there were no tough questions asked by Senators Cruz, Lee, Hawley, Schmidt, or others. Only they know why they stayed out. Senator Wicker prevailed, and the President lost.

Then there is the bizarre situation in Oklahoma. Someone yesterday asked me if I knew what Senator Armstrong was doing. My response was, "Who is Senator Armstrong?" He is the temporary senator appointed to fill Senator Mullins's seat. As Mike Fragoso relays, Armstrong is blocking the nomination of Zach West to the District Court in Oklahoma. This is all about some sort of squabble between West and defeated-AG Drummond. Armstrong returned a blue slip but is now trying to take it back. That's not how things work. If Armstrong prevails here, the President will lose.

Circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state. It bothers me that "home state" senators introduce circuit court nominees. That pageantry reinforces the wrong message. Hiland's seat does not belong to Arkansas and Butler's seat does not belong to Mississippi.

Unfortunately, Trump's surrender here has created a terrible precedent. Should the Republicans ever again return to power, I would hope this entire process is reconsidered. Circuit court nominees should be treated as "at large" seats. Senators can make recommendations, but they cannot dictate who is picked. Worse, judges (like Southwick) should not be allowed to make these deals. We should not tolerate incentive structure where motivated actors can control who represents an entire circuit. Maybe the better approach is to start consulting with all the Senators in a given circuit on possible picks, and then pick the best athlete.

Window insulation kits offer an affordable way to cut the cost of your energy bill and make your home less drafty. For those who can’t afford to replace their windows, these kits are a great alternative.

Most window insulation kits work the same way, by attaching a sheet of heat-shrink plastic or other insulating material to the window panes with double-sided tape or magnetic strips. But since they don’t all perform equally well, we put several of the most popular options to the test in our own homes. Based on those tests, we chose the 3M Indoor Window Insulator Kit as the best overall option for its relatively easy installation and the fact that a single kit covers multiple windows.

Read on for shopping considerations when selecting this type of window treatment and to learn why these are among the best window insulation kits available.

Bottom line: Window insulation kits are an affordable way to reduce energy costs and drafts, with the 3M Indoor Kit leading the pack for its ease and coverage.

Windows that have been treated with insulation cannot usually be opened, meaning these kits are a seasonal solution to drafty windows. The following recommendations are among the best options available in their respective categories.

This 3M insulator kit comes with enough film to cover up to five windows measuring 5 feet long by 3 feet wide. This relatively thick film provides enhanced insulation thanks to its thickness of 0.75 mils (a unit of measurement equal to a thousandth of an inch). The film comes in one cut-to-fit sheet that measures 17.5 feet long by 5.16 feet wide. This kit also comes with a 27.7-yard roll of double-sided tape to facilitate installation and ensure it stays in place all season.

This was my favorite kit to install. I thought I would prefer the rolls of plastic sheeting, and it is true that this one was tricky to lay out and cut to size, but nonetheless, this kit allowed me to reposition the plastic a few times before pressing it down and heating it. Also, the kit does cover a lot of square footage, but the ends of the sheet can be tough, so it’s important to take your time. After I finished installing the kit, removing wrinkles was extremely easy. This kit provided the best results alongside the other 3M products that use the same plastic.

Read our full review: 3M Indoor Window Insulator Kit

What our tester says: “This was my favorite kit because I could reposition the film before pressing it into place, even though laying out and cutting the large sheet took some patience. Once it was up, the wrinkles came out easily with heat, and the finished results were among the best.”—Tom Scalisi, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the 3M indoor window insulation kit at Amazon.

Cozy as the winter months can be, the cold outside can be brutal.

To keep a home insulated and warm in the winter, consider the Duck Max Strength window kit. It comes with everything required for insulating 5-foot-long by 3-foot-wide windows in bedrooms, offices, kitchens, and more, including film, tape, and an instruction manual. But it can be cut to fit smaller windows if necessary.

Made with puncture-resistant shrink film, this 126-inch-long by 62-inch-wide indoor option is perfect for high-traffic homes with children and pets. It’s easy to install and remove cleanly, making it suitable for first timers. For added reliability, this kit can be used on painted wood, aluminum, vinyl, and finished/varnished wood, but it can’t be used on plaster, drywall, or unfinished wood.

To be fair, no film stood a chance against my dog, but it did stick to the windowsill that he has effectively destroyed over the past year. I was able to easily repair any damage with packing tape. Also, the Duck kits come in rolls, which are easy to cut to width and then drop down over the window for easy unfolding. It was really difficult to get the wrinkles out (it took over 30 minutes of heating with a blow dryer to get it reasonably clear), but it was easy to remove once I could get under the tape and pull it back.

Get the Duck Brand Max Strength window insulation kit at Amazon.

Those who want to insulate on a budget can trust this shrink film kit from Duck Brand. With its crystal-clear shrink film and included double-sided insulating tape, this option can reduce energy consumption. At 210 inches long by 62 inches wide, this large film can be cut if required but works best for windows that measure 5 feet long by 3 feet wide. For convenience, this option is also offered in various size options.

This pick can also be applied to painted wood, aluminum, vinyl, and finished wood for more insulation, but it isn’t suitable for plaster, drywall, or unfinished wood varieties.

The kit was fairly easy to install, and it seemed reasonably durable. The roll-out installation made it manageable to unravel, and it featured quality adhesive tape that stuck well and was easy to remove the backing from. While it’s similar in thickness to most of the films we tested, it felt smoother out of the box. It also had a more substantial, higher-quality feel. Unfortunately, it was difficult to remove the existing wrinkles, and there were marks from the manufacturing plant in the film that I could not heat out.

Get the Duck Brand shrink film window insulation kit at Amazon.

If shoppers prefer to install insulating film on the outside of windows, they’ll want a long-lasting product that can hold up to the elements. This outdoor-use window film was created by 3M for that very purpose. Capable of covering up to two 5-foot-long by 3-foot-wide windows, 3M’s kit comes with a sheet of 0.75 mil-thick film that’s 7 feet long and 5.16 feet wide. It also includes just under 14 yards of high-quality double-sided tape. This kit installs like an indoor window film kit: cut, tape, shrink, and trim.

The only difference I could discern between this kit and the other 3M insulation kits was that the adhesive felt like it was of a better quality (though there was nothing wrong with the quality of the other kits). Otherwise, it was the same thickness with the same ease of wrinkle removal. The only challenge I found was that it was difficult and frustrating to install a sheet outside if there was any wind at all, so 3M might consider using a roll-type installation for this kit. But in my opinion, there is no reason it can’t be installed on an interior window as well, so it’s a good kit all around.

New insulating tape is essential for those who love to reuse their insulation sheets. When new insulation is needed, Yotache’s high-density foam tape is a good option. This thick tape comes in two rolls, providing a combined 13 feet of length. It can be cut with ease using a scissors or blade.

The closed cell foam is made from chloroprene rubber foam and neoprene, making it weather- and dustproof, oil- and corrosion-resistant, and flame-retardant. As for the adhesive quality, this tape has a waterproof grid backing that can endure temperatures ranging from -58 to 302 degrees Fahrenheit. Though these are meant for windows, they can also be attached to furniture, cabinets, cars, boats, sports equipment, HVAC systems, plumbing, and more. Plus, there are a lot of thicknesses and lengths to choose from based on the user’s needs.

I installed the Yotache weather stripping at the bottom of one of my windows to see how well it worked. My windows are new and not leaky, so the tolerances were a little tight (though I was able to lock the sashes). However, if I did have leaky windows, I wouldn’t hesitate to buy this foam. It’s incredibly tough thanks to the fiberglass adhesive mesh on the back, yet it’s easy to cut and install. It also removes cleanly but won’t fall off on its own. Plus, there’s a benefit to being able to open the window if necessary. I found the foam too dense for my application, but I can see it making a world of difference for older windows with too much clearance.

Get the Yotache window insulation tape at Amazon.

Comfort aside, one of the most important reasons to insulate drafty windows is to save energy and lower monthly heating costs. Saving energy also benefits the environment. With Frost King’s window film, the company claims users can reduce their carbon footprint related to heating and cooling by up to 35 percent. This kit comes with enough individual sheets of plastic to cover up to nine windows measuring 5 feet long by 3 feet wide. It also includes 165 feet of double-sided tape.

This kit is very similar to other kits on the list, but that’s okay because they’re all good quality. I found that this one installed just like the others, yet with slightly smaller sheets that were a little easier to manage. The film is the same thickness and quality as most of the other kits, and considering it can cover up to nine windows, it’s a great deal. The wrinkles were very easy to remove with a blow dryer, but I did find the tape wasn’t as high quality as the kits from other brands.

Get the Frost King window insulation kit at Amazon.

The StangH Portable Thermal Insulated Blackout Curtains didn’t meet my expectations. First, the way the suction cups are affixed to the curtain with keyrings is extremely frustrating and time-consuming. Also, unless the glass is warm, sticking a suction cup to a cold surface is very difficult. This curtain also looks terrible from the outside, as the suction cups are extremely visible. A standard thermal curtain will likely work almost as well, look much nicer, and be easier to install.

I wanted to ensure that any window insulation kit we recommended was truly effective and easy to install, so I put each of these kits to the test. I installed each kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions to see how easy they were to install and to determine the components’ quality. I also tested how well the plastic shrank and how easy the wrinkles were to remove. I left them on the windows for 2 days to see how well they worked (I even left a few on permanently to get through the winter). I then removed them to determine what that process was like and how much cleanup there would be.

It’s worth noting that without a laboratory full of expensive machinery and repeatable, consistent conditions, it’s hard to objectively determine which window insulation kits insulated better. However, all the kits we included on this list were effective at stopping any noticeable air movement or condensation.

There are a number of factors to consider when shopping for window insulation kits. They’re available in different foil types, such as plastic, magnetic, and reflective. Features like film thickness, dimensions, reusability, and installation requirements will determine which insulation kit is most suitable for your home.

Several window insulation product types are on the market: plastic film, magnetic barriers, and reflective foil insulation.

Windows come in all sizes, so look for kits with enough film to cover your windows. Most kits come with enough plastic sheets and double-sided tape to seal several windows. It’s essential for shoppers to know their windows’ dimensions to determine which kit will work for their home.

Window insulation kits create a trap for air between the window and the film. That trap is called an air lock. Double-sided tape, which holds the film in place on the window pane, will create an air lock. By pressing the film firmly onto the tape, users can create a strong bond that keeps drafts out.

To create a long-lasting seal, durable film is a must. Durability is often determined by the film’s thickness. Thick film offers more resistance to punctures from kids or pets. It’s also easier to apply correctly, thus establishing a good seal. Thick film does a better job of insulating windows. Standard window film is about 19 micrometers (μm) thick, while heavy-duty film can be as thick as 38 μm.

Some homes have only one or two truly drafty windows, while others have a slew of them. Choose a kit that has enough film to cover all the drafty windows. Many kits come in multipacks that can cover up to 10 windows. They come with sheets of film that can be cut to size, so every window that needs insulation can be covered.

Window insulation kits are meant to be temporary solutions to drafty windows. The good news is that most of these kits are reusable, so buyers won’t have to purchase a new kit every year. Films 19 μm or thicker can be peeled off the double-sided tape, folded up, and stored when winter is over. The double-sided tape won’t be reusable, but a roll of double-sided tape is cheaper than a houseful of window kits.

The best window insulation kits are effective, affordable, and easy to install. Most kits are installed by placing double-sided tape around the perimeter of the window jamb. Then, window film is applied to the tape. At the bottom of the window, the film is attached to a piece of tape on the sill, making a seal. Finally, the film is heated with a handheld blow dryer to create a transparent, airtight seal free from wrinkles.

Still have questions about choosing the best window insulation kits? Here’s some more information to help you decide.

Window insulation kits create an effective barrier preventing cold air from entering a home. Heat-shrink film applied to the window pane with double-sided tape creates an air gap that works like a thermal window.

Insulated curtains do a good job of keeping the cold temperatures at bay, but they don’t create airtight seals to hold back drafts like window insulation kits do. Plus, insulated curtains must be closed to work, so they block natural light. Window insulation film is usually clear, so it doesn’t block those precious rays of winter sun from shining into a home.

Some window insulation kits claim to reduce a home’s energy consumption by up to 35 percent. Users will need to install these products carefully and on every leaky window to maximize their effectiveness.

#7787. This Trending Home Feature Is More Practical Than Pretty

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 8, 2026 11:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Each year, Zonda publishes an annual Cost vs. Value (CVV) report, ranking the most common home renovation projects across the nation by return on investment (ROI) value. For the first time, backup power generators entered the top 10 ranking on the list at number 7, with ROI exceeding 100 percent in hurricane-prone and storm-affected regions.

We wanted to understand why home backup power is more popular than ever, since it’s long been considered a luxury upgrade as opposed to an essential part of modern home preparedness. Here’s what several home generator experts and real estate pros think are the reasons why homeowners and homebuyers are now prioritizing backup power and whole-home generators when it comes to home value.

Before we dive into the reasons more people are opting to have a standby generator or whole-home backup generator, it’s important to understand exactly what it does and how it functions. Permanently installed outside a home, a standby generator produces enough electricity to power an entire house indefinitely in the event of a power outage. It connects directly to the home’s electrical panel and uses the natural gas line for fuel. One of the major benefits is that a standby generator automatically turns on within seconds of the power going out, seamlessly transferring the power source from the grid to the generator.

A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances. It has outlets so you can power several appliances. However, it only functions as a temporary power source when the electricity shuts off, making it less reliable than a standby generator. It’s also noisier, requires setup each time you use it, and needs to be refueled periodically.

This whole-home standby generator features a dual-fuel design and a transfer switch that automatically kicks on when the power goes out.

A rise in storm frequency and severity plays a role in more people wanting a backup generator for their home. “Outages stopped feeling rare,” says Beau Tyrrel, product training manager at Jackery. “The average U.S. customer lost about 11 hours of power in 2024, nearly double the decade before. When something happens twice as often, people start planning for it.”

Bert Woidan, operations manager at Trademark Electric, a Generac PowerPro Prestige dealer in Ocala, Florida, recognizes how generator sales are a storm-driven market. “I believe with the increase in weather-related power outages, it only makes sense that more homeowners would want a backup generator with their home,” he explains. “When our company first started selling generators over 20 years ago, I remember standing in the parking lot talking with our founder, and we set a goal to install at least one generator a week. Today, we order generators by the semi load, and during a busy storm season, we’re installing two to three generators a day.”

More storms mean more stress over potential damage. “Especially in our region, if you lose power, the biggest concern is your AC going out,” notes Woidan. “With how humid it gets, it’s not just uncomfortable, but the humidity and moisture can damage your home very quickly, so it’s super important to keep your AC running even if you lose power.”

In the Midwest, the big fear is the basement, says Omar Muhammad, owner of Excel Electrical Technologies in Orland Park, Illinois. “Most homes in our area have a sump pump, and the storms that knock out power are the same storms that send water toward your foundation.” A finished basement can take on tens of thousands of dollars of damage in one night if the pump stops, so buyers and residents understand that a generator protects the most expensive square footage in their house.

Technological innovation has been a game changer for how Americans live. Homes depend on electricity in ways they didn’t 20 years ago, says Muhammad. “A lot of people work from home now and some run medical equipment. Many have an EV in the garage; a high-efficiency furnace that won’t run without power; and a smart thermostat, security system, and Wi-Fi network they rely on every day,” he explains. “An outage is a lot different than it used to be—now it can mean you can’t work, can’t heat the house, and can’t charge your car.” Therefore, a standby generator has become a non-negotiable addition for many homeowners who can’t afford to have their power shut off for any period of time.

Standby generators are now recognized as being as necessary as smoke detectors and security systems, adding value to a home. According to Briggs & Stratton, a permanently installed generator could get you a 3 to 5 percent boost to your home value. And they are now more widespread and becoming the norm, so buyers expect to see them. “Most new builds automatically include a backup generator installation in the blueprints,” notes Woidan.

From a resale perspective, a home generator can help a property stand out by offering buyers peace of mind, especially in neighborhoods that have experienced repeated power disruptions, says Dell Jeanty, founder of Dell Residential Group in Arlington, Virginia. “A home with a generator during an outage demonstrates preparedness, which can be a meaningful selling point,” says Jeanty. “Some estimates suggest standby generators can recover as much as 95 percent of their installation cost at resale, although the actual return depends on the market, installation costs, and buyer demand.”

Curb Appeal Updates You’ll Appreciate Even If You Aren’t Selling Your Home

Curb appeal does not have to be solely cosmetic. See which good-looking projects we are prioritizing to make homes safer, more energy-efficient, and weather resistant.

#7786. Eco-Friendly Hardscaping Ideas for a More Sustainable Garden

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

It’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

With 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

Some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, new pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is important to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

It’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available new materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Whether you’re planning a new patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

Mark Dwyer owns Landscape Prescriptions by MD and is the garden manager for the Edgerton Hospital Healing Garden in Edgerton, Wisconsin. He previously served as director of horticulture at Rotary Botanical Gardens in Janesville, Wisconsin, for 21 years.
